draft.title: Perceived performance: the response-time clock behind skeleton, labor illusion, and the loading.tsx boundary
draft.principle_summary: Perceived latency is not one technique, it is a decision tree gated by a single clock. Nielsen's three response-time limits (0.1s, 1.0s, 10s; T1, Nielsen 1993, replicated over roughly thirty years of prior human-factors research) set WHEN each device is warranted: under about 0.1s no feedback is needed at all, the result itself is the feedback; between about 0.1s and 1.0s the user notices the delay but flow is unbroken and still needs no interstitial; between about 1.0s and 10s the system must show it is working or the user starts to doubt the action registered, this is where skeleton screens and labor illusion belong; past about 10s flow is already broken and the interface owes a percent-complete or a time estimate, not just an activity signal. This clock is the missing anchor: it explains why a loading.tsx that flashes for 80ms is itself a jank source (the skeleton becomes the thing the eye has to process) and why the same boundary is mandatory once a route's data fetch plausibly crosses the 1s line. Skeleton screens (T2, Mejtoft, Langstrom and Soderstrom 2018, ECCE, controlled A/B test) beat spinners on perceived speed and perceived ease of navigation, but the same study found spinner users were FASTER at completing the actual task on first visit, so the win is affective (feels faster), not a task-time gain, and it depends entirely on the skeleton matching the arriving layout (Solen's existing lock is the tested-good variant). Labor illusion (T2, Buell and Norton 2011, Management Science, five experiments) shows visible system effort ("Verfuegbarkeit wird geprueft...") is preferred to an identical instant result, because visible work reads as service quality, not delay, this is the mechanic behind naming the step instead of showing a bare skeleton on search/availability waits over roughly 1s. Progress bars (T2, Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell 2010, CHI) shift perceived duration by roughly 10 percent through animation curve alone and only apply to a real determinate wait, a fabricated bar is taste-rule-1 (no fabricated data) with a stopwatch attached. Optimistic UI is a correctness tradeoff (CONV, not a perception study): safe where reversal is cheap and visible (hearts, saves), banned where reversal is expensive or invisible (payments, bookings), exactly Solen's existing rule. One correction to the file's own prior treatment: the "skeletons are 30 percent faster" figure repeated across vendor blogs has no traceable primary source and should not be cited as a magnitude, only the qualitative and task-tested claims above should be. Route coverage is the generative gap this stream surfaces: 7 of 172 page.tsx have a sibling loading.tsx, an asymmetric pattern across sibling category pages means some routes get the Suspense boundary and functionally identical siblings do not, which is not a taste choice, it is an unaudited accident, and the fix is a rule keyed to the same clock (a route needs loading.tsx when its data dependency can plausibly exceed roughly 1s, matches the final grid/card layout when it has one, and stays absent, not present-but-blank, when the fetch is reliably sub-1s).

sources.claim: Three response-time limits for interactive systems: about 0.1s reads as instantaneous (no feedback needed beyond the result), about 1.0s is the threshold below which the user's flow of thought stays uninterrupted though the delay is noticed, about 10s is the limit for keeping the user's attention on the task before it needs a percent-complete indicator.
sources.source: Jakob Nielsen, Usability Engineering (1993), ch. 5; restated at nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits

sources.claim: Skeleton screens score higher than spinners on perceived speed and perceived ease of navigation in a controlled A/B test, but spinner users completed the underlying find-the-article task faster on first visit, so the skeleton advantage is affective, not a task-time gain.
sources.source: Thomas Mejtoft, Arvid Langstrom, Ulrik Soderstrom, "The effect of skeleton screens: Users' perception of speed and ease of navigation", ECCE 2018 (ACM Digital Library, doi 10.1145/3232078.3232086)

sources.claim: Visibly showing a system doing work (operational transparency / the labor illusion) increases perceived value and can make users prefer a longer, visibly-worked wait over an identical instant result.
sources.source: Ryan W. Buell, Michael I. Norton, "The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value", Management Science 57(9), 2011, pp. 1564-1579 (five experiments)

sources.claim: Progress bar animation pattern (not just presence) changes perceived duration by roughly 10 percent; decelerating/backward-filling patterns read as fastest.
sources.source: Chris Harrison, Brian Amento, Stacey Kuznetsov, Robert Bell, "Rethinking the Progress Bar", ACM UIST/CHI 2010

sources.claim: The commonly repeated figure that skeleton screens make sites feel about 30 percent faster than an identical page with spinners is a vendor/blog-circulated number with no traceable primary study; it should not be cited as a magnitude.
sources.source: No named primary source found across vendor and blog citations (roast.page, UX Collective, onething.design, etc. repeat the figure without attribution); flagged as unsourced, not as a tier claim

sources.claim: Optimistic UI (render success immediately, reconcile with the server, roll back on failure) is a UX convention for masking latency, not an empirically measured perception effect; its safety depends on how cheap and visible a rollback is, not on a study.
sources.source: Named convention, widely documented pattern (e.g. Apollo/React Query optimistic-update docs); no controlled perception study attached

sources.claim: Solen currently has a loading.tsx route boundary on 7 of 172 page.tsx routes.
sources.source: Repo measurement: find app -name loading.tsx (7 hits) vs find app -name page.tsx (172 hits), run this session

draft.solen_current: RATIONALE.md section 20 (Domain 16: states and feedback), lines 745-749, already carries a "Perceived performance (each claim flagged)" block: skeletons flagged contested against "NN/g and controlled tests" without naming the study, the skeleton-matches-final-layout lock recorded as the tested-good variant; progress bars cited to "Harrison 2010, CHI" at roughly 10 percent, correctly tiered T2; labor illusion cited to "Buell and Norton 2011" with the correct one-line mechanism; optimistic UI recorded as CONV with the hearts-safe / payments-banned split already matching current HeartButton behavior. Section 12's folklore table (RATIONALE.md:261) also carries "Skeleton screens always beat spinners" as Contested, pointing back to the same section 20 entry. None of this cites Nielsen's response-time limits anywhere in the file (grep for "Nielsen" and "0.1" / "response time" in RATIONALE.md returns nothing), so the four bullets read as four independent, disconnected flags rather than branches of one clock. The loading.tsx route-boundary count (7 of 172) does not appear anywhere in RATIONALE.md, LOCKFILE.md, or SOURCE.md.
draft.gap: Two gaps, both under the existing "partial" coverage. First, a missing generative anchor: the four perceived-performance claims (skeleton, progress bar, labor illusion, optimistic UI) are recorded as independent flagged facts with no shared framework for WHEN each applies, so a builder has no way to decide "does this specific route need a skeleton, a labor-illusion string, both, or neither." Nielsen's three-limit clock is the standard, T1, and entirely absent; adding it turns four disconnected bullets into one decision rule keyed to elapsed time. Second, a missing computable audit finding: the route-level Suspense/loading.tsx boundary is the actual mechanism that renders "skeleton matching the final layout" in Next.js App Router, and its real-world coverage (7 of 172 page.tsx, asymmetric across sibling category pages per the stream's own framing) is not recorded anywhere in the design-system docs, so there is no standing rule that would catch a new route shipping without one, or flag a route that has one it does not need (sub-1s fetches, where a flashed skeleton itself becomes the jank).
draft.proposed_addition:
Insert into RATIONALE.md section 20, replacing the current four-bullet "Perceived performance" block (lines 745-749) with an expanded version, same location, same section, no other section renumbered:

"**Perceived performance: the response-time clock (T1 anchor, Nielsen 1993).** Three thresholds govern every device below: under about 0.1s, no feedback is needed, the result is the feedback (a flashed-then-gone skeleton here is worse than nothing, it becomes the thing the eye has to parse). Between about 0.1s and 1.0s, the user notices the wait but flow stays unbroken, still no interstitial required. Between about 1.0s and 10s, the system must show it is working or the user starts doubting the tap registered, this is the exact window skeletons and labor illusion occupy. Past about 10s, flow is already broken and the UI owes a percent-complete or a time estimate, not just an activity signal.

- Skeletons (T2, Mejtoft, Langstrom and Soderstrom 2018, ECCE, controlled A/B test, replacing the previous unnamed 'NN/g and controlled tests' citation): beat spinners on PERCEIVED speed and ease of navigation, but the same study found spinner users completed the actual task faster on first visit, so the win is affective, not a task-time gain. Depends entirely on shape-matching the arriving content; Solen's lock (skeleton matches final layout) is the tested-good variant. Do not cite a specific percent-faster figure for skeletons, the commonly repeated 30-percent number has no traceable primary source (flagged MYTH-adjacent, drop it if it surfaces in copy or a deck).
- Labor illusion / operational transparency (T2, Buell and Norton 2011, Management Science, five experiments): visible system effort ('Verfuegbarkeit wird geprueft...') is preferred to an identical instant result. Applies inside the 1-10s window on search/availability waits; naming the step beats a bare skeleton there. Probe-able (Taste Lab candidate below).
- Progress bars (T2, Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell 2010, CHI): animation curve shifts perceived duration by roughly 10 percent; only where a real determinate wait exists, a fabricated bar is taste rule 1 (no fabricated data) with a stopwatch on it.
- Optimistic UI (CONV, tradeoff, not a perception study): saves/hearts safely optimistic (current HeartButton), payments and bookings never optimistic, correctness risk is the sacrifice and here it is unacceptable.

**The loading.tsx boundary is the response-time clock made computable.** Next.js App Router resolves the 1s-to-10s window at the ROUTE level: a page.tsx without a sibling loading.tsx has no Suspense boundary, so any fetch inside it that crosses roughly 1s renders a blank tab with no activity signal at all, silently violating Nielsen's second threshold. Repo measurement this session: 7 of 172 page.tsx have a sibling loading.tsx, an unaudited, asymmetric pattern (some category-page siblings covered, functionally identical others not) rather than a deliberate choice. Rule, generative default for any route work: add a loading.tsx (skeleton shaped to the arriving grid/list/card, per the existing lock) when the route's data dependency can plausibly exceed about 1s (a search/listing query, an external API call, anything not a cache-hit); leave it absent, not present-but-blank, when the fetch is reliably sub-1s (a static or fully-cached page), since a boundary that flashes under the 0.1s line adds jank it claims to remove. This is an audit-and-backfill item, not a redesign: existing skeleton shapes are reused per-route, only the coverage gap closes.

**Taste Lab probe:** on 2-3 real Solen routes currently missing loading.tsx where the fetch is a genuine 1-3s search/availability query (candidate: salon search results, availability check on the booking flow), A/B the bare skeleton against a labor-illusion string over the same skeleton ('Verfuegbarkeit wird geprueft...' vs. silent skeleton), read for perceived-wait rating and whether users self-report noticing anything at all, per Buell and Norton's method. This is the only claim in this block that is genuinely probe-worthy on our own data, everything else (Nielsen's clock, skeleton shape-matching, optimistic-UI correctness boundary) is a structural rule, not a hypothesis to test."

Cross-reference, not duplicate: PSYCHOLOGY.md law 8 (first-100ms-is-the-brand, Google/Deloitte 2020, +0.1s load speed correlates with +8.4% conversion on mobile retail) owns the CONVERSION angle of speed; this addition owns only the PERCEPTUAL/display angle (how a wait feels once it is already happening), and should link to law 8 by name rather than restate its number.
draft.taste_lab_probe: On 2-3 real routes with a genuine 1-3s wait (salon search results, booking availability check) that currently ship a bare skeleton with no loading.tsx or a silent one, A/B a labor-illusion string over the skeleton ("Verfuegbarkeit wird geprueft...") against the silent skeleton alone. Measure self-reported perceived wait and whether users notice the wait unprompted, following Buell and Norton's (2011) experimental method. This is the one claim in the addition that is a hypothesis to calibrate on Solen's own users, not a structural rule to just apply.

claim_verdicts.claim: Nielsen's three response-time limits: ~0.1s instantaneous, ~1.0s flow uninterrupted, ~10s attention limit.
claim_verdicts.note: Verified via NN/g (nngroup.com/articles/response-times-3-important-limits) which restates Nielsen, Usability Engineering (1993) ch.5. Numbers and framing match the draft exactly. Solid T1.

claim_verdicts.claim: Skeleton screens beat spinners on perceived speed/ease of navigation but spinner users completed the task faster on first visit.
claim_verdicts.note: Verified: Mejtoft, Langstrom, Soderstrom, ECCE 2018 (36th European Conference on Cognitive Ergonomics), doi 10.1145/3232078.3232086. Search confirms both findings (higher perceived speed/ease for skeletons, faster first-visit task completion for spinners). Correctly tiered T2, single study not meta-analysis.

claim_verdicts.claim: Labor illusion: visible system effort increases preference for a longer wait over an identical instant result.
claim_verdicts.note: Verified: Buell and Norton, Management Science 57(9), 2011, pp.1564-1579, five experiments (online travel and dating domains), HBS-hosted PDF confirms. Correctly tiered T2.

claim_verdicts.claim: Progress bar animation pattern shifts perceived duration by roughly 10 percent, cited as Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell, 2010, CHI.
claim_verdicts.note: CITATION ERROR, not a magnitude error. 'Rethinking the Progress Bar' by Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell was published at UIST 2007, not CHI 2010 (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1294211.1294231). The 2010 CHI paper with a similar theme, 'Faster Progress Bars: Manipulating Perceived Duration with Visual Augmentations,' has a DIFFERENT author list: Harrison, Yeo and Hudson, no Amento or Kuznetsov. The draft conflated the two papers' author list and venue/year. The ~10-11 percent magnitude itself checks out (search confirms the 2007 paper found the backward-rippling pattern made the wait feel about 11 percent shorter, p<0.001), so the qualitative claim survives, but the citation must read 2007, UIST, not 2010, CHI. Corrected in verified_addition.

claim_verdicts.claim: The commonly repeated 'skeletons make sites feel ~30% faster' figure has no traceable primary source.
claim_verdicts.note: Confirmed: search of vendor/blog sources (UX Collective, dev.to, freecodecamp) repeats generic skeleton-screen enthusiasm but none surface a named 30%-magnitude study; NN/g's own skeleton-screens article does not cite this figure either. Draft's own flagging as MYTH-adjacent and 'do not cite' is correct and should stay.

claim_verdicts.claim: Optimistic UI is a correctness-tradeoff convention, not a measured perception effect.
claim_verdicts.note: Correctly tiered as convention, no perception study attached, matches how the draft uses it (correctness/reversal-risk framing, not a magnitude claim).

claim_verdicts.claim: 7 of 172 page.tsx have a sibling loading.tsx in the Solen repo.
claim_verdicts.note: Re-ran `find app -name loading.tsx | wc -l` (7) and `find app -name page.tsx | wc -l` (172) in this worktree; count reproduces exactly. This is a repo measurement, not a literature claim, tier stays CONV/repo-fact.

None of the ten banned myth_screen numbers (2000% samples, 70-90% defaults, losses-2x, jam-study, $300M button, 5%-retention-25-95%-profit, retention-5-25x-cheaper, Amazon-100ms-1%-sales, Duolingo +20% DAU, UGC-4x) appear anywhere in this draft. The draft's PSYCHOLOGY.md law-8 cross-reference correctly uses the approved substitute for the Amazon anecdote, 'Google/Deloitte 2020: +0.1s = +8.4% conversion,' exactly as the myth_screen table prescribes. The 30% skeleton figure is a new unlisted myth candidate, correctly self-flagged by the draft rather than cited as fact.

myths_caught: 'Skeleton screens make sites feel ~30% faster than spinners' -- unsourced vendor/blog figure, correctly flagged by the draft as do-not-cite, MYTH tier, kept out of verified_addition as a magnitude.

Citation conflation, not a pop-stat myth but a factual error worth flagging alongside myths: the progress-bar 10-percent finding was attributed to 'Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell, 2010, CHI' when that exact author list published at UIST 2007; the 2010 CHI paper on the same topic has a different author list (Harrison, Yeo, Hudson). Corrected to 2007, UIST in verified_addition.

verified.residual_risks:
One real citation error was caught and fixed: the progress-bar study was attributed to "Harrison, Amento, Kuznetsov and Bell, 2010, CHI" but that author list published "Rethinking the Progress Bar" at UIST 2007; CHI 2010 belongs to a different paper by a partly different author list (Harrison, Yeo, Hudson). Fixed to 2007/UIST in verified_addition, magnitude (~10-11 percent) unaffected. Everything else in the draft held: Nielsen's three limits, the Mejtoft skeleton study, the Buell and Norton labor-illusion study, and the 7-of-172 loading.tsx repo count all verified against live sources or a fresh repo run.

Not a myth-screen issue but worth a QUESTIONS.md flag for the owner: the proposed rule ("add loading.tsx when a route's fetch can plausibly exceed ~1s") is a generative default, not a frozen literal, so it does not touch LOCKFILE.md. But it does imply future engineering work (auditing which of the 165 uncovered routes actually need a boundary) that this stream does not scope or prioritize, someone has to decide which routes get audited first and whether that is worth doing before or after other roadmap items. Also worth flagging: the Taste Lab probe (labor-illusion string vs silent skeleton) touches live booking-flow copy, so it needs the mockup-first / owner-approval path before any A/B ships, this addition only proposes the hypothesis, not permission to test it live.
